title: Database Internals
summary: How a relational database actually works under the hood — page layouts, B-trees and LSM-trees, WAL and crash recovery, buffer pools, query optimization, MVCC, and the engine-level patterns behind modern cloud databases.

chapters.title: How Databases Are Built
chapters.summary: DBMS architecture from first principles — the storage, transaction, and query subsystems; the read/write/space amplification trade-offs (RUM conjecture); and the design choices that shape every engine.

chapters.title: Storage Engines: B-Trees
chapters.summary: The page-oriented storage engine that has dominated OLTP for 40 years — page layout, slotted pages, splits and merges, B+ tree variants, copy-on-write, and concurrent B-tree patterns (Blink-trees, latch coupling).

chapters.title: Storage Engines: LSM-Trees
chapters.summary: The log-structured storage engine behind RocksDB, LevelDB, and Cassandra — memtables, SSTables, flush and compaction strategies (size-tiered vs leveled), tombstones, Bloom filters, and the read/write/space amplification trade-offs.

chapters.title: Write-Ahead Logging and Recovery
chapters.summary: How databases survive crashes — ARIES, redo and undo, log sequence numbers, checkpoints, dirty page tables, group commit, WAL archiving, and the three-phase recovery dance after kill -9.

chapters.title: Buffer Management
chapters.summary: The DB's in-memory page cache — buffer pool sizing, replacement policies (LRU, Clock), pinning, dirty pages, background writers, direct I/O, and the double-buffering pitfalls of mixing OS and DB caches.

chapters.title: Indexing
chapters.summary: Every flavour of index that ships in modern databases — primary vs secondary, clustered vs non-clustered, covering, composite, partial, expression, inverted, bitmap, and hash — plus the cost of maintaining them.

chapters.title: Query Execution
chapters.summary: How a query plan actually runs — the Volcano pull-model, vectorised batch execution, JIT-compiled execution, and the operators that show up in every plan (scans, joins, aggregates, sorts).

chapters.title: The Query Optimizer
chapters.summary: The brain of the database — turning declarative SQL into a physical plan via rule-based and cost-based optimization, statistics and histograms, join ordering, dynamic programming, and the cost-gap reality.

chapters.title: Concurrency Control
chapters.summary: How the engine keeps concurrent transactions from corrupting each other — isolation level semantics (dirty reads, write skew, phantoms), lock managers (2PL, S2PL, modes, granularity), MVCC version chains, deadlock detection, and SSI.

chapters.title: Transactions and Durability
chapters.summary: ACID under the hood — single-node commit protocols, group commit, the fsync gotchas, force/no-force and steal/no-steal buffer policies, the (Steal, No-Force) ARIES choice, savepoints, and snapshot bloat.

chapters.title: Replication and Failover
chapters.summary: Why replicate and how the engine actually does it — single-leader / multi-leader / leaderless taxonomy, streaming replication, physical vs logical replication, Postgres replication slots, hot vs warm standby, and failover orchestration.

chapters.title: Distributed Transactions
chapters.summary: Transactions across multiple machines — a consensus refresher (Paxos, Raft, FLP), 2PC and its coordinator-failure problem, 3PC, Paxos commit, Spanner's TrueTime + external consistency, distributed snapshot isolation, and the saga alternative.

chapters.title: Modern Database Patterns
chapters.summary: Engine-level innovations of the 2020s — compute-storage separation (Aurora, Neon), HTAP engines (TiDB, SingleStore), vectorised columnar engines (DuckDB), embedded DBs (SQLite, LMDB), pgvector internals, multi-master engines, and NVMe-aware designs.
